cues.text: A Church Built Like a Tomb
The Basilica of St. Stephen at Neuvy-Saint-Sépulcre , in the Indre region of central France, was founded in the early eleventh century.
Lord Eudes de Déols established it on returning from his own pilgrimage to Jerusalem, deliberately building it on the round plan of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
This design intended to let French pilgrims unable to make the journey themselves still walk, in miniature, the same sacred ground.
On July 15, 1257, Cardinal Eudes of Châteauroux , returning from the Crusades in the Holy Land, presented the church with two drops of what tradition holds is Christ's own Blood.
The drops were gathered at Calvary during the Passion, together with a fragment of his tomb.
The relic is described in the church's own tradition as coagulated but pure, uncontaminated by water or earth in its gathering.
The community has long held this detail to distinguish it from other Precious Blood relics venerated elsewhere in medieval Europe.
Several of those relics carry more disputed or contested accounts of their own origin.
In 1621, the Archbishop of Bourges, André Frémiot, founded a Confraternity of the Most Precious Blood at Neuvy.
Two years later, Pope Gregory XV granted new indulgences to those who honored the relic there.
The parish still keeps Easter Monday and the first of July each year as days of solemn Mass and procession in the relic's honor.

As with several of the Precious Blood relics venerated across medieval Europe, the exact circumstances of the relic's first-century origin rest finally on tradition rather than independent documentary proof.
What can be said with confidence is that this particular relic has been venerated continuously at Neuvy-Saint-Sépulcre since a cardinal's own hand delivered it there in 1257.
That devotion has now outlasted, by more than seven and a half centuries, the very age of Crusade and pilgrimage that first carried it the length of Christendom to reach its resting place.
